sections.title: Part 1
sections.transcript:
Receptionist: Riverside Arts Centre, how can I help?
Caller: Hello, I'd like to join the beginners' pottery course.
Receptionist: Of course. Can I take your surname?
Caller: It's Whitlock, W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.
Receptionist: Thank you. The class meets on Thursday evenings, starting at six thirty.
Caller: And how much is the course?
Receptionist: It's eighty-five pounds for eight weeks, clay included.
Caller: Do I need to bring anything?
Receptionist: Just an apron. We provide everything else. The studio is number fourteen, behind the library.
Caller: Is there a dress code?
Receptionist: You must wear closed shoes because of the heavy tools. Parking is free after five pm. Your tutor is Elena, and the course ends with a small exhibition of your work.

sections.title: Part 2
sections.transcript:
Guide: Welcome to Millbank Riverside Park. It was a rail yard until the 1990s, which is why the paths are so straight. This year two facilities are new: the bike hire stand and the boat tours that leave from the jetty. The cafe and the playground have been here for years.
Now, to find your way: the visitor centre is the building next to the main gate, marked C on your map. The cafe is on the corner by the river, A. Bike hire is at the far end of the lawn, E, and the toilets are beside the playground, F.
Volunteers do most of the planting, usually on Saturdays. The park is busiest in summer, but the best time for birdwatching is early morning. Tours last forty minutes, and the only thing you cannot do in the park is light a barbecue.

Priya: So our project is rooftop beekeeping. Who's doing what?
Marcus: I'll contact the council about permits. You're better at the survey, Priya.
Priya: Fine, I'll design the questionnaire. And we should both visit the apiary on campus next week.
Marcus: Agreed. Then you write the introduction and I'll prepare the slides.
Priya: Now the stages. First, we select a sunny terrace for the hives.
Marcus: Second, buy protective suits. Third, record the weight of each hive every week.
Priya: Then compare honey yield between seasons.
Marcus: And finally present everything in a poster rather than slides at the fair.

sections.title: Part 4
sections.transcript:
Lecturer: Today, seed dispersal by ants, or myrmecochory. Many plants attach a fatty structure called an elaiosome to their seeds. Ants carry the seed to their nest, eat the fat and discard the seed on a waste heap. This protects it from seed-eating beetles, and the soil around the nest is rich in nutrients. Ants typically move seeds no more than ten metres.
In Australia the practice is most common in heathland. Researchers marked seeds with paint to follow them. A problem is that some invasive ants eat the seeds instead of burying them, so conservationists now place seeds close to the nests of native ants.
